name: Runcorn Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Mersey at Runcorn Gap on Runcorn Railway Bridge, opened in 1868 and also known as the Ethelfleda Bridge. The first passenger train crossed it on April 1st 1869, and it is now a Grade II* listed building.

name: Allerton Hall
text: Your train passes near Allerton Hall, on the train's {side}, a Palladian house built in about 1736. The abolitionist William Roscoe bought it in 1795; it stands in Clarke's Gardens and is now a pub.

name: Hunts Cross station
text: Hunts Cross station, at one end of this stretch, opened in May 1874 and is a listed building. It was the only station with four platforms on the Cheshire Lines Committee's route between Liverpool Central and Manchester Central.

name: Hough Green station
text: Hough Green station, at one end of this stretch, opened on May 1st 1874 and is a listed building. Five years later it became a junction, when a line was opened just to the east.

name: Widnes War Memorial
text: Your train passes near Widnes War Memorial, on the train's {side}, a Portland stone obelisk in Victoria Park unveiled in 1921. It cost less than the money raised, and the rest went to a fund for the town's poor.

name: St Luke's Church, Farnworth
text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church, Farnworth, on the train's {side}. A chapel was first built here in about 1180, dedicated to St Wilfrid, when the village was known as St Wilfrids-on-the-Hill; it was renamed St Luke's in 1859.

name: Warrington West station
text: Warrington West station, at one end of this stretch, opened on December 16th 2019, after a second bid to the government's New Stations Fund succeeded where the first had failed. It has parking for 287 cars.

name: Warrington Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Warrington Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1750 as Bank Hall, a house designed by James Gibbs. Its cast-iron gates, made at Coalbrookdale, had been shown at the International Exhibition in London in 1862.

name: St Elphin's Church, Warrington
text: Your train passes near St Elphin's Church, Warrington's parish church, on the train's {side}. Tradition says the first church here was built in the 7th century for Elphin, its first priest; the spire, added in a Victorian restoration, is 281 feet (86 metres) high.

name: Padgate station
text: Padgate station, at one end of this stretch, has a station building of the Cheshire Lines Committee's usual design. It now houses a fish and chip shop.

name: Risley Moss
text: Your train passes near Risley Moss, on the train's {side}, a country park and Site of Special Scientific Interest. It is one of the last fragments of the raised peat bogs that once covered large parts of south Lancashire and north Cheshire.

name: Irlam station
text: Irlam station, at one end of this stretch, dates from 1893. The Manchester Ship Canal, opened the next year, needed the railway raised to let ships pass, so a new line was built alongside at a higher level and the old station closed.

name: St Michael's Church, Flixton
text: Your train passes near St Michael's Church, Flixton, on the train's {side}, on high ground near the River Mersey. A church here is recorded from at least 1198, and its churchyard has gravestones going back to 1669.

name: Flixton House
text: Your train passes near Flixton House, on the train's {side}, built in 1806. When its owner closed footpaths across his estate in 1826, the people of Flixton took him to court and won, in one of the first footpath battles in England.

name: Urmston station
text: Urmston station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1873. Its Victorian ticket office on the Liverpool-bound platform, disused for years, reopened as a pub and restaurant in 2008.

name: Humphrey Park station
text: Humphrey Park station, at one end of this stretch, opened on October 15th 1984, built by British Rail as an experiment. It has no station building at all.

name: Kellogg's Manchester Plant
text: Your train passes near Kellogg's Manchester Plant, on the train's {side}, where building began in 1937 as the first factory on the Barton Dock Estate. During the Second World War it was the largest food factory in Europe.

name: Old Trafford
text: Your train passes near Old Trafford, on the train's {side}, home of Manchester United since 1910 and the largest club football stadium in the United Kingdom. Bobby Charlton called it the “Theatre of Dreams”.

name: Liverpool Road station
text: Your train passes near Liverpool Road, on the train's {side}, the world's oldest surviving terminal railway station. It opened on September 15th 1830 as the Manchester end of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, and is now part of the Science and Industry Museum.

name: Manchester Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Manchester Cathedral, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the Perpendicular Gothic style after a college of priests was founded here in 1421. Its nave roof is held up by carved angels with gilded instruments.

name: Chetham's Library
text: Your train passes near Chetham's Library, on the train's {side}, the oldest free public reference library in the English-speaking world, in use since 1653. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels met there when Marx visited Manchester in 1845.

name: National Football Museum
text: Your train passes near the National Football Museum, on the train's {side}, in the Urbis building. The museum began at Preston North End's Deepdale ground and moved to Manchester in 2012.

name: Etihad Stadium
text: Your train passes near the Etihad Stadium, on the train's {side}, built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games. Manchester City moved here from Maine Road in the summer of 2003, after it was converted into a football stadium.

name: Site of Hyde Road
text: Your train passes near the site of Hyde Road, on the train's {side}, home of Manchester City and the clubs before it from 1887 to 1923. Until 1896 there were no changing rooms, so players changed in a pub, the Hyde Road Hotel.

name: Store Street Aqueduct
text: Your train passes near Store Street Aqueduct, on the train's {side}, built in 1798 by Benjamin Outram to carry the Ashton Canal. It crosses the street at a skew of 40 degrees, and is believed to be the oldest aqueduct of its kind in Britain still in use.

name: London Road Fire Station
text: Your train passes near London Road Fire Station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1906 in red brick and terracotta. As well as the fire station, it housed a police station, an ambulance station, a bank and a coroner's court.

name: Beetham Tower
text: Your train passes near Beetham Tower, on the train's {side}, a 47-storey skyscraper finished in 2006 on a sliver of land at the top of Deansgate. Until 2018 it was the tallest building in the United Kingdom outside London.

name: Slade Hall
text: Your train passes near Slade Hall, on the train's {side}, a small Elizabethan manor house begun in 1583. An inscription above the porch dates it to 1585.

name: Church of St Nicholas, Burnage
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Nicholas, Burnage, on the train's {side}, a Modernist brick church of 1930 to 1932 by N. F. Cachemaille-Day. Pevsner called it “a milestone in the history of church architecture in England”.

name: Parrs Wood House
text: Your train passes near Parrs Wood House, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century Georgian villa. From 1825 it was the home of the MP and philanthropist James Heald; in the 1920s it was sold to Manchester Corporation on condition it was used for education.

name: The Towers, Didsbury
text: Your train passes near The Towers, on the train's {side}, built between 1868 and 1872 for John Edward Taylor of the Manchester Guardian. It later became the home of the engineer Daniel Adamson, where the Manchester Ship Canal was first planned in 1882.

name: Barnes Hospital
text: Your train passes near Barnes Hospital, on the train's {side}, a Victorian Gothic building on a mound, finished in 1875. It was a convalescent hospital, founded with a gift of £10,000 from the philanthropist Robert Barnes, and closed in 1999.

name: Manchester Airport station
text: Manchester Airport station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1993 with the airport's second terminal, on a short branch from the Styal line. A third platform opened in 2008, and trams arrived in 2014.

name: Apprentice House, Quarry Bank
text: Your train passes near the Apprentice House at Quarry Bank, on the train's {side}, built by Samuel Greg in 1790 for the children apprenticed at his cotton mill. The mill kept child apprentices until 1847.

name: St Bartholomew's Church, Wilmslow
text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church, Wilmslow, on the train's {side}. A church here is first recorded in 1246; most of the present building is from the early 16th century, and it is Grade I listed.

name: St Philip's Church, Alderley Edge
text: Your train passes near St Philip's Church, Alderley Edge, on the train's {side}, begun in 1851 as the Manchester architect J. S. Crowther's first independent work. Pevsner called it “large, ambitious, and unmistakably prosperous-looking”.

name: Chorley Old Hall
text: Your train passes near Chorley Old Hall, on the train's {side}, the oldest inhabited country house in Cheshire. Its moated medieval range was built in about 1330, and an Elizabethan range was added in the 16th century.

name: Lovell Telescope
text: Your train passes near the Lovell Telescope at Jodrell Bank, on the train's {side}. When it was finished in 1957 it was the largest steerable dish radio telescope in the world; it is now the third largest.

name: Twemlow Hall
text: Your train passes near Twemlow Hall, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century country house on the site of an older moated manor house. It was owned by the Booth family from the 16th century until the 19th.

name: St Luke's Church, Holmes Chapel
text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church, Holmes Chapel, on the train's {side}. It began in about 1430 as a timber-framed church with a sandstone tower; in the early 18th century its nave and chancel were encased in brick.
